title: Frequently asked questions
lede: Visiting a store, shopping with Star Buds, and the cannabis basics.
disclaimer: General information, not medical or legal advice. Rules differ by state and can change; check your store's page before you visit.

items.q: What do I need to bring on my first visit?
answer: At the Oklahoma stores: “All visitors must be at least 18 years of age with a valid medical card and must provide a valid photo ID. We take cash and debit cards and there is also an ATM inside our dispensary for your convenience.”
At Star Buds Baltimore: “All visitors must be at least 21 years of age and must provide a valid photo ID. We take cash and there is also an ATM inside our dispensary for your convenience.”
Requirements differ by state, so check your store's page before you go.

items.q: Do I need a medical card?
answer: It depends on the state. Mississippi and Oklahoma run medical cannabis programs, so buying there requires a valid medical card. Maryland and New York allow adult-use purchases for anyone 21 or older with a valid photo ID, and both also run medical programs.

source.basis: State-program facts stated generally, as REVISION-1 R1.4 allows (Mississippi and Oklahoma: medical programs; Maryland and New York: adult-use 21+ and medical), with the required general-information note. Consistent with the captured store copy: Oklahoma visit answers require 'a valid medical card'; the Baltimore visit answer requires visitors to be 'at least 21 years of age'.

items.q: What is the difference between THC and CBD?
answer: THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol) and CBD (cannabidiol) are the best-known cannabinoids in the cannabis plant. THC is the main intoxicating compound, the one that causes a high. CBD is not intoxicating in the way THC is. Product labels list how much of each a product contains.

source.basis: Neutral general information; no health claims.

items.q: What do indica, sativa and hybrid mean?
answer: They are traditional names for cannabis plant types: indica plants tend to be short and bushy, sativa plants tall with narrow leaves, and hybrids are crosses of the two. Shops still use the labels to group strains, but how a product feels depends more on its cannabinoid and terpene content, and on the person, than on the label.

source.basis: Neutral general information; no health claims.

answer: Terpenes are aromatic compounds made by many plants, cannabis included. They give each strain its scent, from citrus to pine to pepper. Common ones include myrcene, limonene and pinene, and some lab-tested products list their terpenes on the label.

source.basis: Neutral general information; no health claims.

items.q: How are edibles different from smoking?
answer: Start low and go slow. Eaten cannabis is processed through the digestive system, so its effects come on much more slowly than smoking or vaping and can last longer. Wait until the first serving has taken full effect before having more.

source.basis: Neutral general information; 'start low and go slow' is the only dosing guidance, per REVISION-1 R1.4.

items.q: How should I store cannabis at home?
answer: Keep it in its original child-resistant packaging, locked away or out of reach and out of sight of children and pets. Edibles can look like ordinary sweets, so keep them apart from food. A cool, dark, dry place also keeps products fresh. If a child or pet swallows cannabis, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or your vet.

source.basis: Neutral safety information. 1-800-222-1222 is the US national Poison Help line (America's Poison Centers).
